items.title: 1. Why vascular patients are different: disease biology, organ reserve and risk
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 1.1 The vascular patient has a systemic disease, not merely a surgical lesion

- Atherosclerosis is a chronic, inflammatory, lipid-driven disease of the arterial intima.
- Endothelial dysfunction permits lipoprotein retention, macrophage recruitment and development of a fibrous or lipid-rich plaque.
- Progressive stenosis reduces flow reserve: resting blood flow may remain sufficient, but exercise, hypotension, anaemia and increased tissue demand expose the limitation.
- Plaque rupture or erosion causes platelet activation, thrombosis and acute occlusion.
- Calcification makes vessels difficult to clamp, cannulate and reconstruct; diffuse atheroma increases embolic and access-related risk.

- The coronary, carotid, renal, mesenteric and leg circulations share these mechanisms.
- A patient presenting for an infrainguinal bypass may therefore have silent coronary disease, impaired LV relaxation, carotid plaque and CKD.
- Vascular surgery adds major physiological stresses—rapid afterload changes, ischaemia–reperfusion, blood loss, anticoagulation and inflammatory activation—to pre-existing limited reserve.
- Preventing myocardial infarction or kidney injury is not a matter of choosing an anaesthetic drug in isolation: it is about preventing excessive demand or inadequate supply while treating the underlying disease.

- Aneurysmal disease is related but distinct.
- An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a full-thickness dilatation involving structural degradation of elastin/collagen and altered wall mechanics.
- Atherosclerosis commonly coexists, but aneurysm expansion is not simply an atherosclerotic stenosis.
- Dissection begins when blood separates aortic wall layers through an intimal tear or intramural haemorrhage.
- A type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and threatens the coronary arteries, aortic valve and pericardium; type B originates distal to the left subclavian artery and threatens the distal organs through true-lumen compression, branch-vessel obstruction or rupture.
- These mechanisms determine whether the appropriate immediate response is anti-impulse therapy, operative repair or haemorrhage control.

## 1.2 Distinguish the major clinical syndromes before planning anaesthesia

| **Syndrome** | **What has failed?** | **Typical clues** | **What changes management?** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intermittent claudication | Exercise-related skeletal-muscle perfusion reserve | Reproducible calf/thigh/buttock pain relieved by rest | Walking programme, smoking cessation, vascular risk treatment; revascularisation for persistent lifestyle-limiting symptoms |
| Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) | Resting tissue perfusion, usually with multilevel disease | Ischaemic rest pain, ulcer or gangrene for >2 weeks; diabetes may mask pain | Limb viability, infection, angiographic anatomy, patient risk, conduit availability |
| Acute limb ischaemia (ALI) | Abrupt arterial inflow loss | Sudden pain, pallor, coldness, pulselessness, sensory and motor deficit | Rutherford class and urgency of revascularisation; immediate UFH unless contraindicated |
| Symptomatic carotid stenosis | Artery-to-artery embolism or flow failure | Ipsilateral retinal or hemispheric TIA/minor stroke | Recent symptoms and degree of stenosis, infarct size, timing and treatment risk |
| AAA | Loss of aortic structural integrity | Usually asymptomatic; occasionally abdominal/back pain or rupture | Size/growth, symptoms, anatomy, fitness, suitability for EVAR versus open repair |
| Acute aortic syndrome | Aortic wall disruption | Abrupt severe chest/back/abdominal pain, pulse deficits, neurological or organ malperfusion | Type A versus B; complicated versus uncomplicated; CTA anatomy |

- **Clinical distinction:** claudication is not synonymous with limb-threatening ischaemia, and a cool pulseless limb is not automatically irreversible. Loss of motor function is particularly ominous in acute ischaemia. Conversely, a patient with diabetes and sensory neuropathy may have advanced tissue loss while reporting little pain.

## 1.3 Quantifying peripheral disease and whole-patient risk

- A focused vascular history asks about walking distance, rest pain, tissue loss, prior grafts, amputations, carotid symptoms, coronary symptoms, functional capacity, smoking, diabetes, renal impairment, dialysis timing, frailty, infection and previous complications of anaesthesia.
- Examine heart and lungs, volume status, peripheral pulses, skin temperature, wounds, bilateral pressures, neurological function and dialysis access.
- Document **baseline** limb power, sensation and pulses because postoperative change is a critical finding.

- The ankle–brachial index (ABI) is ankle systolic pressure divided by the higher brachial systolic pressure.
- An ABI ≤0.90 supports PAD; values <0.40 indicate severe perfusion impairment, but values alone do not define CLTI.
- Noncompressible calcified arteries, common in diabetes and CKD, may yield spuriously high ABI (>1.40); toe pressures, toe–brachial index, pulse volume recordings and duplex are then more informative.
- Toe pressure <30 mmHg or ankle systolic pressure <50 mmHg suggests severe ischaemia in an appropriate clinical context.
- Duplex identifies lesion location and graft patency; CT or MR angiography provides a procedural map but introduces contrast or MRI-device considerations.

- A vascular operation is frequently an elevated-risk noncardiac procedure.
- Estimate cardiac risk with a validated method (e.g. RCRI, NSQIP/MICA), recognise the limitations of these scores in complex aortic operations, and assess functional capacity using history or the Duke Activity Status Index when feasible.
- Poor functional capacity, frailty and cardiovascular disease predict harm, but routine stress tests for every vascular patient are inappropriate.
- Obtain a test only if it is clinically indicated and would change management, e.g. prompt investigation of active cardiac symptoms or a genuinely beneficial revascularisation.
- The September 2026 reaffirmation of the AHA/ACC perioperative cardiovascular guideline confirms the substance of the 2024 recommendations without changing them [1].

**Find unstable disease first:**

- An acute coronary syndrome, decompensated heart failure, unstable tachy- or bradyarrhythmia, severe symptomatic valve disease or uncontrolled infection may require treatment before elective repair.
- Urgent threatened-limb or ruptured-aneurysm surgery cannot usually wait for exhaustive optimisation; that is why readiness for physiological deterioration is central to vascular anaesthesia.

### Focused investigations and how they alter a plan

- **ECG** for rhythm, conduction, previous infarction, LV hypertrophy and active ischaemic change. An ECG is not a test of coronary perfusion reserve.
- **Hb, platelet count, coagulation studies and group-and-crossmatch** proportional to anticipated blood loss and anticoagulant exposure; assess iron deficiency and correct anaemia when there is sufficient lead time.
- **Creatinine/eGFR, potassium, glucose/HbA1c** for contrast planning, dialysis timing and drug adjustments; a normal creatinine in a frail patient does not exclude impaired GFR.
- **TTE** when symptoms, examination or prior findings suggest significant ventricular or valvular pathology; focus on EF and filling/diastolic function, RV performance, significant stenosis, and pulmonary pressure rather than simply “normal echo”.
- **Risk-directed troponin and natriuretic peptides** may assist assessment and postoperative surveillance in high-risk patients. Interpret troponin trends and clinical context; elevations are not automatically type 1 MI.
- **CTA for aortic anatomy:** proximal neck and iliac access for EVAR, branch-vessel involvement in dissection, landing zones for TEVAR, atheroma burden and possibility of left subclavian coverage. A complex operation cannot be adequately planned without knowing its anatomical extent.

## 1.4 Optimisation is treatment of risk, not a quest for perfect numbers

- Smoking cessation improves cardiovascular and pulmonary health and reduces wound complications.
- Even a short opportunity should trigger cessation support and nicotine replacement as appropriate; longer abstinence generally brings greater benefit.
- Continue statins and appropriate antiplatelet secondary prevention.
- Optimise heart failure without precipitating hypovolaemia.
- Treat significant anaemia and diabetes; ensure appropriate nutrition, mobility and prehabilitation where surgery can wait.
- Control infection and protect tissues with ischaemic ulcers.
- Obtain a shared plan for antithrombotics and neuraxial techniques—stopping an antiplatelet drug may endanger a carotid or peripheral stent, while continuing it may constrain regional approaches.

- **Medication decisions follow the indication and procedure:**

| **Medication** | **Usual perioperative principle** | **Why it matters / important caveat** |
|---|---|---|
| Chronic β-blocker | Continue if tolerated; do not newly start high-dose treatment on surgery day | Avoids rebound tachycardia and ischaemia; aggressive initiation can cause hypotension, bradycardia and stroke (POISE) |
| Statin | Continue and initiate for usual secondary-prevention indications | Reduces ongoing atherosclerotic risk; discontinuation removes long-term protection |
| ACE inhibitor/ARB | For treated hypertension, withholding approximately 24 h before major surgery can reduce induction hypotension; when indicated for HFrEF, continuation may be reasonable | Individualise; hypotension may be dangerous during cross-clamping and carotid surgery; balance against heart failure needs |
| SGLT2 inhibitor | Hold ≥3 days before elective surgery (ertugliflozin ≥4 days); check blood ketones if unwell or urgent | Euglycaemic ketoacidosis can occur during fasting, infection and major vascular stress; normal glucose is not reassuring [1] |
| Antiplatelet(s) | Decide jointly for CEA, CAS, EVAR and limb interventions | Aspirin frequently continues; carotid stenting typically requires dual antiplatelet therapy; a recent coronary stent creates additional risk |
| Anticoagulants | Assess thrombotic indication, renal function, bleeding risk and regional technique | Avoid indiscriminate bridging; use drug-specific and neuraxial timing recommendations |
| Insulin | Continue essential basal insulin with adjusted dosing; monitor glucose/ketones | Prevents insulin-deficient ketosis and reduces infection and wound risk; major cases may require IV insulin |
| Diuretics | Adjust for volume and potassium | Excessive preoperative diuresis can predispose to induction collapse and AKI; withholding may worsen pulmonary congestion |

- Patients on dialysis often benefit from haemodialysis close to surgery, commonly the preceding day, to achieve suitable fluid status and electrolytes.
- Protect an AV fistula arm from BP cuffs, arterial puncture and avoidable cannulation.
- If dialysis occurs shortly before surgery, ask about intradialytic hypotension and residual heparin.
- Do not label renal impairment an automatic indication for large fluid loads: overload may be worse than modest transient renal hypoperfusion.

## 1.5 Why vascular disease amplifies postoperative complications

- Poor skin microcirculation, diabetes, uraemia, malnutrition, tissue oedema and graft implantation increase wound infection and dehiscence risk.
- Impaired peripheral sensation makes positioning neuropathies and pressure injuries harder to detect; carefully protect heels, peroneal nerves, sacrum and the contralateral ischaemic limb.
- Systemic inflammation, hypercoagulability, embolism and haemodynamic lability promote perioperative MI, stroke and AKI.
- Anaesthetic management should protect tissue oxygen delivery while avoiding oedema: adequate Hb, controlled temperature, prompt treatment of hypotension, anticoagulant review, wound care and early recognition of graft compromise are intertwined.
- A technically successful bypass is not a success if the new graft thromboses in recovery or the patient develops an unrecognised compartment syndrome.

## 1.6 An exam-ready perioperative plan for each major comorbidity

**Use this seven-condition framework for SS_VS 1.2:**

- Chapters elsewhere teach the full underlying diseases; these notes must still explain how each condition changes the operation, induction, vascular control and recovery.
- The decision sequence is: identify severity/stability → optimise what can safely be changed → plan perfusion and drug management → monitor for the characteristic postoperative complication.

### Ischaemic heart disease (IHD)

- Before elective surgery, ask about angina frequency, recent ACS/PCI, functional reserve and coronary medications; poor walking distance from claudication is not a direct measure of cardiac limitation.
- Obtain ECG and risk-directed biomarkers; investigate new unstable symptoms, but do not revascularise stable coronary disease solely to lower the risk of a planned vascular operation.
- Continue established β-blockers and statins where tolerated; coordinate aspirin/P2Y12 timing with the coronary and vascular indications.
- During clamping, balance afterload, coronary perfusion pressure, heart rate and haemoglobin; during bleeding or unclamping, avoid sustained hypotension and tachycardia.
- Postoperatively, monitor for silent myocardial injury (serial ECG/troponin where indicated), heart failure and arrhythmia rather than waiting for chest pain [1].

### Cardiac failure and ventricular dysfunction

- Define whether the patient has reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction/LVH, RV failure or important valve disease; ask about orthopnoea, oedema, congestion, recent admissions and exercise tolerance.
- Decompensated HF warrants treatment before elective repair, whereas rupture or threatened-limb surgery requires a rescue-ready plan.
- A stiff LV is preload-sensitive yet vulnerable to fluid overload; a failing systolic LV may deteriorate with the sudden afterload of a high clamp.
- Use arterial monitoring and targeted echo/flow assessment for higher-risk surgery; titrate fluid, vasopressor and inotrope to the mechanism rather than a CVP target.
- Preserve rhythm and coronary perfusion.
- After operation watch for pulmonary oedema, low output, renal injury and myocardial injury [1].

### Arrhythmia and cardiac devices

- Establish the rhythm, haemodynamic consequences, burden of AF, ventricular rate, thromboembolic risk, anticoagulant indication and any pacemaker/ICD dependence.
- Correct significant potassium/magnesium abnormalities and assess recent syncope or unexplained tachycardia.
- Plan anticoagulant interruption/restart around surgical bleeding, procedural heparinisation and regional catheters; routine bridging is inappropriate for most patients.
- Agree device interrogation, electrosurgery and external pacing/defibrillation arrangements where relevant.
- Treat unstable perioperative tachyarrhythmia with immediate resuscitation/cardioversion as appropriate, not prolonged rate-control attempts; evaluate reversible bleeding, ischaemia, hypoxia and electrolyte triggers [1].

### Chronic hypertension

- Assess usual home/clinic pressure, end-organ disease, medications, LVH and any secondary causes.
- A single elevated preoperative measurement is not itself proof of an unstable patient; assess persistence, symptoms, urgency and institutional guidance.
- Continue chronic β-blockade, and individualise ACEI/ARB withholding or continuation by indication, HF status and procedure.
- Avoid profound induction hypotension in a chronically hypertensive patient with impaired autoregulation and do not force the BP to a normal population value during carotid clamping or aortic reperfusion.
- Equally, severe postoperative hypertension after CEA risks hyperperfusion and neck bleeding and should be treated promptly against the agreed patient-specific target.

### Diabetes mellitus

- Identify insulin dependence, recent control, hypoglycaemia, autonomic neuropathy, CKD, infection, vascular ulcers and any SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1/GIP treatment.
- Tailor the fasting, basal-insulin and IV-insulin plan; never omit essential basal insulin in type 1 diabetes.
- Stop SGLT2 inhibitors sufficiently before elective surgery and check ketones in an unwell urgent patient even with normal glucose.
- Monitor glucose throughout long, changing-perfusion operations; a commonly referenced perioperative goal is roughly 5.6–10 mmol/L when safe, adapted to local ADS–ANZCA policy and hypoglycaemia risk [1,29].
- Good glycaemic control supports wound healing; diabetic neuropathy also increases positioning injury and may conceal compartment syndrome.
- Resume medication safely after intake, renal function and ketone risk are reassessed.

### COPD and limited respiratory reserve

- Identify exacerbation, recent lower-respiratory infection, baseline dyspnoea, sputum, bronchodilator and steroid use, hypoxaemia/CO₂ retention, sleep-disordered breathing and pulmonary hypertension.
- Optimise inhalers, treat reversible infection/exacerbation, support smoking cessation and arrange postoperative respiratory care.
- Assess whether open transperitoneal repair, a thoracotomy/one-lung ventilation or prolonged supine IR sedation is tolerable; anatomically suitable EVAR may avoid an open incision but is not automatically safe.
- During GA permit adequate expiratory time and avoid dynamic hyperinflation; balance protective ventilation against venous return, especially during clamping or rupture.
- Plan dynamic analgesia, cough, physiotherapy and an appropriate extubation/HDU strategy.

### Renal failure, CKD and dialysis

- Determine AKI versus chronic CKD, current potassium/bicarbonate, volume balance, residual urine, dialysis modality/time, anaemia, uraemic platelet dysfunction and vascular access.
- Avoid cannulating or compressing an AV fistula arm; check residual dialysis anticoagulation when planning neuraxial/deep blocks.
- Prevent sustained renal hypoperfusion while avoiding pulmonary oedema from routine prophylactic fluid boluses.
- For suprarenal clamping discuss clamp duration and renal/visceral perfusion; after EVAR distinguish renal-branch occlusion from contrast-associated injury.
- Dose-adjust renally cleared agents and avoid unproven “renal-dose dopamine”, prophylactic forced diuresis or dialysis solely to remove contrast.
- Postoperatively monitor potassium, acid–base, urine output and indications for nephrology/RRT support.

- **High-yield distinction:** urgency governs how much optimisation is possible. A stable, symptomatic CAD patient scheduled for elective open AAA repair deserves assessment and risk reduction; a patient with rAAA or Rutherford IIb limb ischaemia needs treatment and physiological preparedness in parallel with immediate repair, not a prolonged cardiac work-up.

items.title: 2. The physiology that governs all aortic surgery: clamping, unclamping and reperfusion
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 2.1 Understanding proximal and distal circulations

- Aortic cross-clamping creates **two different circulatory environments**.
- Proximal to the clamp, pressure and effective arterial impedance rise; distal to it, arterial inflow falls.
- The size of the haemodynamic change depends on clamp level, aortic collateral flow, preload, LV function, vascular resistance and duration.
- A patient with severe LVH and diastolic dysfunction may develop ischaemia or pulmonary oedema from a relatively modest increase in afterload despite apparently “adequate” blood pressure.
- A patient with a failing LV may instead show falling stroke volume and cardiac output despite rising proximal arterial pressure.

- A simplified relationship helps: **MAP ≈ CO × SVR + CVP**, and **CO = HR × stroke volume**.
- An increase in MAP during clamping does not prove adequate CO or microcirculatory oxygen delivery.
- Moreover, the LV faces a sudden change in arterial impedance and wave reflections, not a perfectly steady resistance.
- This is why monitoring the direction of cardiac output, filling and ischaemic signs is more useful than memorising a fixed percentage change in systolic BP.

### Clamp level determines what is ischaemic

| **Clamp level** | **Main physiological issues** | **Why the risks differ** |
|---|---|---|
| Infrarenal | Increased LV afterload; reduced lower-limb/pelvic flow, renal neurohumoral vasoconstriction | Renal arteries remain perfused directly but renal blood flow may fall despite normal proximal pressure; limb/gut ischaemia possible |
| Suprarenal | Above plus interrupted renal perfusion until unclamping | Duration of renal ischaemia becomes a major AKI determinant; renal protection depends on clamp time and collateral flow |
| Supracoeliac | Renal and splanchnic ischaemia; larger proximal haemodynamic stress | Impaired hepatic/mesenteric perfusion, lactate and inflammatory mediator generation; severe reperfusion burden |
| Descending thoracic | Large distal territory including spinal, mesenteric and renal perfusion depending on position | High SCI and multiorgan risk; may require distal perfusion, CSF drainage and neuromonitoring |

- A high clamp can transiently redistribute venous blood centrally and increase LV preload while raising afterload.
- At a later stage of surgery blood loss, venous pooling and reduced distal venous return can reduce central filling.
- There is no universal claim that clamping always raises or lowers cardiac output.
- Assess the patient and clamp position rather than reciting an invariant rule.

## 2.2 Pre-clamp strategy: create reserve without causing fluid overload

- Before clamping, establish reliable, continuously displayed arterial pressure—usually radial arterial cannulation **before** induction in high-risk open aortic cases.
- The patient generally requires two large-bore peripheral cannulae (often 14–16 G), a rapid-infuser and blood availability, appropriate temperature monitoring, urinary catheter and frequent arterial blood-gas/electrolyte testing.
- Central access is useful when peripheral access is inadequate or vasoactive infusions require it; it is not automatically a reliable measure of fluid responsiveness.
- In major thoraco-abdominal repair, the level of repair may justify cardiac output monitoring, TEE and spinal perfusion adjuncts.
- Discuss the precise clamp site, estimated clamp duration, heparin timing, anticipated blood loss and unclamp plan with the surgeon before induction.

- Assess haemoglobin, calcium, base deficit/lactate, temperature, pulmonary oedema and current vasopressor requirements.
- Replace **demonstrable deficits** with balanced crystalloid or blood products, not a fixed prophylactic bolus.
- A useful fluid challenge is a small 200–250 mL aliquot with reassessment of stroke volume, arterial trace, capillary refill and signs of pulmonary congestion.
- If bleeding is present, red cells and haemostatic components restore oxygen carriage and coagulation more effectively than large volumes of crystalloid.
- Establish noradrenaline availability and a strategy for hypertension (for example titrated glyceryl trinitrate or an alternative vasodilator according to LV function).

- When the team is ready to clamp, reconfirm volume status, depth of anaesthesia, heart rate and ECG ST trend, temperature and distal organ protection plan.
- Ask the surgeon for a verbal announcement before application.
- **Why:** an abrupt increase in LV wall stress increases myocardial oxygen demand just as coronary flow may be compromised by tachycardia or low diastolic perfusion pressure.

## 2.3 Clamp application and maintained clamping

- Initially, MAP and proximal systolic pressure usually rise and LV wall stress increases.
- Treat clinically important hypertension if accompanied by ischaemia, ventricular strain or dangerous pressure, but do not automatically reduce pressure to “normal” if a high clamp requires proximal perfusion of the heart and brain.
- First check anaesthetic depth, analgesia, hypercarbia and other causes of sympathetic stimulation.
- If left ventricular function is adequate, vasodilators can attenuate the afterload increase; use short, titratable agents and reassess CO.
- When a weak LV fails under new impedance, an inotrope or altered vascular strategy may be preferable to indiscriminate vasodilation.

- Continuously look for **myocardial ischaemia** (new ECG change, regional wall-motion abnormality, falling output, pulmonary congestion), distal perfusion failure, temperature loss, coagulopathy and increasing lactate.
- If a high clamp compromises renal or visceral perfusion, the decisive variable is often **ischaemic duration**—not a renal-protective diuretic.
- Communicate any unexpected deterioration immediately; consider clamp repositioning or use of distal perfusion when surgically feasible.
- The longer the clamp, the more likely distal tissue accumulates lactate, potassium, CO₂ and inflammatory mediators.

**Heparin:**

- Systemic UFH (often 70–100 units/kg for large arterial clamping, with some teams using different doses or ACT-guided regimens) may be requested before clamping; follow the surgeon's agreed protocol and measure ACT when appropriate.
- Where bleeding risk is exceptional, balance thrombosis against bleeding.
- Protamine reversal is guided by total heparin administered, timing, ACT/clinical bleeding and the risk of hypotension or anaphylactoid reactions.
- A milligram of protamine neutralises approximately 100 units of recent unfractionated heparin; accumulated metabolism and local protocols mean a full calculated dose may be excessive.

## 2.4 Unclamping: why dramatic hypotension can occur

- Unclamping reverses the proximal afterload increase, exposes a large dilated distal vascular bed, permits venous pooling and suddenly returns acidic, hyperkalaemic blood to the central circulation.
- The acute **fall in preload** and SVR can reduce MAP and myocardial perfusion; myocardial depression, acidaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypocalcaemia may add to the fall.
- Some organs have reactive hyperaemia, whereas microvascular no-reflow and endothelial injury can sustain distal malperfusion despite macrovascular restoration.
- The resulting shock is not simply “hypovolaemia,” so the response must be diagnostic as well as therapeutic.

- Prepare several minutes before release.
- Communicate the anticipated time and ask for staged clamp release where possible.
- Reassess fluid responsiveness and haemorrhage losses.
- Give a small volume or blood-product bolus only if needed; avoid filling an already congested LV.
- Reduce an unnecessary vasodilator, prepare a titratable noradrenaline infusion or boluses and confirm adequate ionised calcium.
- Consider a blood gas immediately before and after release.
- After release monitor the ECG and rhythm, ETCO₂, lactate, pH, K⁺, ionised Ca²⁺, haemoglobin and peripheral pulses.
- A transient fall in ETCO₂ from reduced pulmonary blood flow can accompany hypotension, while later rising ETCO₂ may reflect washout of stored CO₂.
- Persistent low ETCO₂ requires assessment of CO, ventilation and embolic events.

### Practical response to severe hypotension after unclamping

- **1.** Ask the surgeon whether bleeding, clamp release or proximal obstruction is responsible; check the field and measured blood loss. Ensure oxygen delivery and a useful arterial trace.
- **2.** Treat immediately threatening hypotension with a vasopressor while rapidly differentiating low preload, vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, arrhythmia and haemorrhage. Noradrenaline is commonly appropriate for vasodilatory shock; if there is marked cardiac failure, address inotropy.
- **3.** If haemorrhage or fluid responsiveness is present, give warmed blood/crystalloid in assessed aliquots and re-evaluate; in heavy bleeding activate MHP rather than giving litres of saline.
- **4.** If widening QRS, peaked T waves, bradyarrhythmia or VF accompanies high K⁺, give IV calcium promptly, followed by potassium-shifting therapy and definitive control of ongoing K⁺ release. Acidosis is treated by restoring perfusion; sodium bicarbonate is not a substitute for correcting shock.
- **5.** Consider temporary surgical reclamping or staged reperfusion in refractory deterioration **only through immediate surgical discussion**. Repeat sampling and closely observe limb, renal and bowel perfusion.

### A worked physiological example

- A 72-year-old undergoing infrarenal AAA repair has MAP 76 mmHg and CO 4.2 L/min before clamping.
- After clamping, MAP rises to 102 but CO falls to 3.3.
- A superficial interpretation would celebrate the “improved” pressure.
- In reality, the LV is failing to sustain flow at the increased afterload, raising myocardial oxygen demand while reducing forward oxygen delivery.
- Priorities are ECG/echo evaluation, avoiding tachycardia, titrating afterload and maintaining coronary perfusion—not administering fluid until a CVP target is reached.
- Upon release, MAP suddenly falls to 52 with CO 3.0 and a new lactate rise.
- Assess blood loss and volume responsiveness, support vascular tone and examine contractility before assuming the entire fall is due to a saline deficit.

## 2.5 Reperfusion is an organ-specific problem

**Limb:**

- Oedema increases compartment pressure and reduces capillary flow; reperfusion can cause hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria, AKI and arrhythmias.
- **Bowel:** mucosal injury promotes bacterial translocation, inflammatory shock and later colonic ischaemia.
- **Kidney:** ischaemia/reperfusion, atheroembolism and inflammatory injury act on a background of CKD.
- **Spinal cord:** interruption of radicular/segmental arteries, low perfusion pressure and disrupted collaterals may cause immediate or delayed paralysis.
- The correct response after a technically successful repair is therefore structured surveillance, not merely extubation and transfer.

## 2.6 Prolonged limb versus gut ischaemia: distinctive physiology and rescue

**Skeletal muscle ischaemia:**

- Arterial interruption depletes ATP, impairs Na⁺/K⁺ pumps and produces intracellular calcium accumulation, anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis.
- Reperfusion introduces oxygen free radicals, endothelial activation and capillary leakage into confined fascial compartments.
- Potassium, acid, phosphate and myoglobin entering the circulation can cause brady/ventricular arrhythmias, vasoplegia and pigment-associated AKI.
- Prior collateralisation changes tissue tolerance: a chronically ischaemic limb may react differently from a suddenly embolised normal limb.
- Duration, baseline neurological deficit and degree of muscle damage matter more than a reassuring global MAP or return of a distal pulse.

**Mesenteric and colonic ischaemia:**

- Supracoeliac clamping directly interrupts major splanchnic inflow; even infrarenal repair can threaten colonic collateral supply through inferior mesenteric, internal iliac or marginal-artery pathways.
- Low cardiac output, prolonged hypotension, haemorrhage, vasoconstriction and atheroembolism can cause non-occlusive or arterial mesenteric ischaemia.
- Hypoxic mucosal barrier failure followed by reperfusion promotes oedema, bacterial/endotoxin translocation, local thrombosis and systemic inflammation.
- Ischaemic colitis may appear after an apparently technically successful graft repair.
- Lactate may be normal initially and is not sensitive enough to exclude an evolving bowel catastrophe.

**Recognition and response:**

- Record exact clamp/occlusion duration and compromised territories.
- During operation discuss distal perfusion, temporary shunting, clamp relocation or expediting anastomosis when feasible; maintain perfusing pressure and cardiac output while preventing excess fluid-related bowel oedema.
- Before and after reperfusion trend ECG, K⁺, blood gases, Ca²⁺, lactate, urine output and limb compartment findings.
- After aortic repair, new disproportionate abdominal pain, ileus, bloody diarrhoea, distension, increasing lactate or unexplained shock requires immediate vascular/general surgical review and appropriate CTA, endoscopy or operation; do not merely treat the acidosis.
- After limb revascularisation assess for compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis as in Chapter 9. These are different tissue emergencies, despite a shared ischaemia–reperfusion mechanism.

items.title: 3. Elective open aortic and aorto-iliac surgery

items.body:
## 3.1 What operation is actually being performed?

- Open repair of an infrarenal AAA usually proceeds through a midline transperitoneal or retroperitoneal approach.
- The surgeon gains proximal and distal control, administers systemic heparin as planned, cross-clamps the aorta and iliac arteries, opens the sac, evacuates thrombus, ligates bleeding lumbar branches and sews a tube or bifurcated synthetic graft to suitable aortic/iliac segments.
- The clamp is released after de-airing/flushing and inspection of anastomoses.
- The sac and retroperitoneum are closed over the graft.
- Bifurcated grafts or aorto-bifemoral bypass for occlusive disease require more extensive distal dissection and may add time, blood loss and limb-ischaemia risk.
- Aortic surgery becomes physiologically different if the clamp must be moved above the renal or visceral arteries, or if thoracotomy, one-lung ventilation, left-heart bypass or cardiopulmonary support are required.

- The operation's main physiological phases are: **induction**, **dissection and haemorrhage**, **heparinisation**, **clamp application**, **distal ischaemia**, **graft anastomosis**, **staged release**, **reperfusion**, and **haemostasis/closure**.
- Understanding their sequence anticipates when blood loss, hypertension, renal injury and hypotension occur.
- In open aorto-iliac occlusive surgery, the dominant issue may be prolonged ischaemia and severe background CAD rather than aneurysm rupture.

### Preoperative decision: open versus EVAR

- For an asymptomatic degenerative AAA, repair decisions incorporate symptoms, rate of expansion, sex, size, life expectancy, surgical risk and feasibility of standard endograft sealing.
- A 5.5 cm diameter is a commonly used threshold in otherwise appropriate men; threshold decisions in women are individualised and may favour consideration at smaller sizes because rupture can occur at smaller diameters.
- Do not turn an isolated ultrasound diameter into an automatic instruction to operate: anatomical suitability, competing mortality and patient preferences matter.
- Symptomatic or rapidly enlarging aneurysms demand more urgent discussion.
- The ESVS 2024 AAA guideline remains the reference for this decision [2].

- Open repair avoids endoleaks and the same intensity of lifelong device surveillance but entails greater early physiological stress, ventilation requirements, blood loss and recovery time.
- Endovascular repair reduces early procedural burden in suitable anatomy, but requires adequate landing zones, usable access and indefinite surveillance for sac enlargement, migration, endoleak and late rupture.
- EVAR-1 illustrates an early survival advantage without assured late advantage [16].
- The correct technique is a shared anatomical and risk decision, not a declaration that EVAR is universally preferable in older or frail patients.

## 3.2 Preoperative evaluation specific to open aortic surgery

- In addition to the cardiovascular assessment in Chapter 1, review the CTA with the surgeon: neck, thrombus/calcification, clamp level, renal artery anatomy, accessory renals, inferior mesenteric and internal iliac supply, previous abdominal surgery and planned distal anastomoses.
- Ask about chronic mesenteric ischaemia, prior bowel resections and previous aortic interventions.
- These predict ischaemic bowel and collateral dependence after clamping.
- Check creatinine/eGFR and baseline urine output, haemoglobin, coagulation/antithrombotic status, group-and-crossmatch and lung physiology.
- Severe COPD can make abdominal closure and prolonged ventilation challenging.
- Establish the likely ICU destination and the patient’s wishes concerning a prolonged postoperative course.

- An epidural may improve early dynamic analgesia, coughing and respiratory mechanics after open abdominal surgery but complicates systemic heparinisation, bleeding management and hypotension.
- If used, insert well before heparinisation according to the applicable neuraxial–antithrombotic policy, document an atraumatic placement, and have a planned approach to traumatic/bloody tap, postoperative anticoagulation and catheter removal.
- A bloody tap should prompt **reassessment of the timing and safety of systemic heparin, not an automatic attempt to continue at the original schedule**; consider postponement, alternative analgesia and specialist consultation.
- Routine full-dose systemic anticoagulation in a patient with a traumatic neuraxial placement can create an epidural haematoma with permanent neurological injury.
- Some centres favour non-neuraxial options for high-bleeding-risk aortic cases.

## 3.3 Anaesthetic technique, access and monitoring

- A standard high-risk open repair commonly warrants a preinduction radial arterial line, continuous five-lead ECG with ST monitoring, two dependable large peripheral IVs, blood products and a rapid infuser, urinary catheter, core temperature, regular blood gases and postoperative monitored or ICU care.
- Central access, TEE or other CO monitoring should be based on ventricular impairment, clamp height, access difficulty and anticipated instability rather than routine convention.
- Consider cerebral or spinal monitoring for high thoracic work and plan lower-limb/visceral perfusion assessment if prolonged ischaemia is likely.

- Induction must preserve coronary and cerebral perfusion without excessive tachycardia.
- For a patient with significant LVH and diastolic dysfunction, avoid abrupt vasodilation and underfilling; choose titrated induction doses and a vasopressor ready before loss of consciousness.
- Balanced volatile or propofol-based anaesthesia may be used—there is no reliable evidence that a particular hypnotic overcomes haemorrhage, clamp physiology or untreated CAD.
- Opioid or remifentanil titration reduces sympathetic peaks; maintain appropriate oxygenation and normocapnia unless a specific surgical/neurological reason changes the target.
- Protect renal perfusion by preventing sustained hypotension, not by routine “renal-dose dopamine”, mannitol or furosemide.

### Blood conservation and coagulation

- Major arterial anastomoses and raw surfaces can bleed rapidly.
- **Cell salvage** is often valuable in elective open aortic surgery provided contamination and local contraindications are considered.
- A typical sequence is suction with anticoagulation → reservoir and filtration → centrifugation/washing → reinfusion of washed red cells; it does not replace platelets or coagulation factors.
- Optimise Hb preoperatively, correct hypothermia and acidosis, use careful surgical haemostasis, and obtain fibrinogen, platelets and viscoelastic testing during heavy bleeding.
- Follow a major haemorrhage protocol with guided component replacement, not a single arbitrary haemoglobin trigger.
- Recheck ionised calcium repeatedly during citrate-rich transfusion.
- Do not presume TXA should be given routinely to every vascular case; weigh likely blood-saving benefit, graft thrombosis/embolism risk, renal function and local evidence.
- Heparin/ACT testing and selective protamine reversal are coordinated with the surgeon.

## 3.4 At clamp application and during clamping: make a physiological plan

- The principles from Chapter 2 apply here.
- For **infrarenal repair**, the renal arteries are nominally perfused but there can still be neurohumorally mediated renal vasoconstriction and reduced renal flow.
- For **suprarenal or supracoeliac clamps**, interrupted renal or splanchnic inflow adds time-sensitive ischaemia.
- Record clamp start and finish times.
- Target adequate perfusion at the required territories: proximal pressure alone does not guarantee distal viability.
- Maintain an anaesthetic depth that prevents sympathetic surges without creating hypotension; titrate vasodilators or vasopressors based on myocardial performance.
- The use of a TEE to observe LV filling and function can distinguish rising afterload from fluid overload.
- During a prolonged high clamp, discuss perfusion adjuncts or clamp relocation as needed.

- As the anastomosis approaches completion, communicate preparation for release: reassess volume, blood loss, K⁺, pH, ionised calcium, lactate and vasoactive requirements; anticipate the return of acidic blood and large lower-body vasodilation.
- **An examiner expects a strategy**—for example, small assessed fluid/blood aliquots, a titrated noradrenaline infusion, staged release and repeat ABGs—not the phrase “ensure euvolaemia.” [12]

## 3.5 Postoperative implications and complications

- Aortic graft repair often needs HDU/ICU surveillance for bleeding, myocardial injury, AKI, respiratory dysfunction, bowel ischaemia and leg perfusion failure.
- Serial abdominal examination, lactate trends, urine output and Hb are useful but not specific.
- An elevated lactate after unclamping can represent washout; persistent or worsening metabolic acidosis with abdominal pain/distension, GI bleeding, ileus, pressor requirement or haemodynamic deterioration should raise concern for **mesenteric/colonic ischaemia**.
- An internal iliac or inferior mesenteric collateral problem can make this more likely.
- Early surgical/vascular assessment and CT/endoscopy when appropriate matter more than reassuring oneself that arterial pressure has normalised.

- Other complications: myocardial ischaemia or arrhythmia, graft thrombosis or distal embolism (new pulseless/cold limb), compartment syndrome, pneumonia/atelectasis, abdominal compartment syndrome, AKI, ureteric injury, graft infection, aortoenteric fistula (usually delayed, including GI haemorrhage) and incisional failure.
- Monitor for epidural haematoma in a neuraxial patient, especially if anticoagulation resumes.
- Early extubation is appropriate when awake, warm, stable and haemostatically controlled, but may be unsafe after major blood loss, acidosis, pulmonary oedema, severe COPD exacerbation or extensive high aortic surgery.

### Analgesia after open aortic repair

- A thoracic epidural (often a local anaesthetic plus opioid infusion) can provide strong movement-related analgesia, but monitor sympathetic hypotension and adjust if spinal perfusion or graft flow are concerns.
- If an epidural is contraindicated, options include IV opioid PCA, acetaminophen, selective low-dose ketamine, wound infiltration or abdominal wall catheters/block (e.g. rectus sheath/TAP) depending on incision.
- NSAIDs may be inappropriate in AKI, bleeding, renal artery clamping or heart failure; gabapentinoids increase sedation in frail or renal-impaired patients.
- Treat pain sufficiently for mobilisation and cough while protecting respiratory and haemodynamic reserve.

items.title: 4. Endovascular aortic surgery: EVAR, TEVAR and complex grafts
items.priority: P1 CORE (6 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.los: SS_VS 1.4; SS_VS 1.17; SS_VS 1.18; SS_VS 1.10; SS_VS 1.12; SS_VS 1.2; SS_VS 1.19; SS_VS 1.16
items.body:
## 4.1 The principal advantage is avoiding a large incision and open cross-clamp

- Standard EVAR introduces a stent-graft through femoral/iliac access, positions it below the renal arteries and extends its limbs into the iliac circulation.
- Completion angiography checks graft seal, branch flow, leg perfusion and endoleaks.
- Aorto-uni-iliac configurations may require contralateral iliac occlusion and a femoro-femoral crossover bypass.
- Fenestrated or branched EVAR (F/BEVAR) incorporates visceral or renal artery branches using fenestrations and bridging stents; more complex procedures require longer contrast exposure, substantial access, renal/mesenteric ischaemia precautions and sometimes spinal perfusion measures.

- TEVAR similarly deploys a stent-graft in the descending thoracic aorta.
- It may require coverage of the left subclavian artery, proximal landing near the arch, rapid pacing or transient controlled hypotension for accurate deployment, and lower-body/spinal perfusion planning.
- Endovascular repair avoids an open thoracic aortic cross-clamp but **can still cause spinal cord ischaemia, embolic stroke and visceral ischaemia** from branch exclusion, aortic manipulation and altered collateral perfusion.
- Do not infer “minimally invasive” means “low consequence.”

## 4.2 Preoperative assessment of suitability and risk

- The CTA is a procedural roadmap.
- For EVAR, identify proximal neck length/angulation, thrombus, calcification, iliac vessel diameter and tortuosity, common/internal iliac patency and whether branch-vessel perfusion is threatened.
- Consider prior abdominal aortic repair, renal transplant, dialysis, aortoiliac occlusion and previous access complications.
- In TEVAR, assess arch anatomy, left subclavian/vertebral circulation, extent of coverage, prior abdominal aortic repair, hypogastric flow and whether CSF drainage or a staged approach is being considered.
- For F/BEVAR, clarify renal and visceral stent procedures and risk of prolonged sheath occlusion.

- This is an opportunity to match the expected physiology to the patient: an 82-year-old with frailty, severe COPD, stable CAD and a short-neck AAA may still be unfit for prolonged open repair but anatomically unsuitable for simple EVAR; an elaborate fenestrated plan is not automatically benign.
- Ask whether a conservative pathway, alternative repair or transfer to a higher-volume centre is more appropriate.
- The 2026.1 ANZCA Final SAQ specifically required meaningful cardiac risk assessment and optimisation—not a vague “ECG, echo and cardiology review.” [13]

### Contrast and kidney protection

- Contrast-associated AKI risk increases with pre-existing CKD, intravascular depletion, shock, repeated contrast, atheroembolism and nephrotoxic exposures.
- Pre-procedure creatinine/eGFR and haemodynamic optimisation help; use the smallest diagnostic contrast load that still produces safe technical imaging.
- Avoid routine high-volume crystalloid if the patient has decompensated HF; individualise isotonic hydration for patients with high renal risk who can tolerate it.
- Prophylactic N-acetylcysteine, routine diuretics and dialysis solely to remove contrast are not established protective treatments.
- A newly rising creatinine after EVAR requires distinction among contrast-associated injury, renal artery occlusion, atheroembolism, hypoperfusion and obstruction.
- In a patient with a renal stent or branch graft, sudden oliguria may be a **vascular emergency**, not simply “contrast nephropathy.”

## 4.3 Anaesthesia options and working in the hybrid/interventional suite

- Uncomplicated infrarenal EVAR in a cooperative, haemodynamically stable patient can often be performed with local infiltration plus carefully titrated sedation, neuraxial anaesthesia when safe, or general anaesthesia.
- The decision depends on patient cooperation, access complexity, duration, pain, respiratory disease, antiplatelet/anticoagulant status and need for immediate immobility.
- Local/sedation preserves spontaneous ventilation and may avoid sympathectomy/circulatory collapse, but movement during deployment can displace the graft; a sedated supine patient with large drapes may have an inaccessible airway.
- GA provides immobility and airway control but introduces haemodynamic changes and may delay early neurological assessment.
- Complex TEVAR/FBEVAR often needs GA with intubation, controlled ventilation and haemodynamic precision; specific staged procedures may use awake monitoring.

- **Set up the room as an anaesthetic location—not a radiology room with an anaesthetist added late.** Confirm oxygen, suction, anaesthesia machine, capnography, defibrillator, blood access, heater, airway cart, infusion pumps, emergency drugs and call-for-help plan.
- Assess difficult patient access from the head after the C-arm moves; arrange extension tubing and pump location outside the radiation field.
- Wear lead apron, thyroid shield and eye protection as required, use lead screens and minimise fluoroscopy exposure.
- The principles are time, distance and shielding: staff exposure falls with distance and appropriate shielding; keep hands out of the primary beam.
- Check radiation dose reporting and escalation thresholds with the procedural team.
- Beware cables/surgical drapes interfering with monitoring or airway access, and limited support after hours.
- ANZCA professional standards for anaesthesia outside operating theatres apply [7].

### Typical monitoring

- Standard anaesthesia monitors and temperature remain mandatory.
- An arterial line is strongly favoured for major TEVAR/FBEVAR, ruptured EVAR and haemodynamically fragile cases.
- Bilateral pressures may help when brachiocephalic vessels are manipulated and when left subclavian coverage changes left-arm readings.
- Have large-bore peripheral access and ready blood for access-vessel or aortic rupture.
- A central line and CO/TEE monitoring depend on cardiac function and procedure; do not cannulate solely by habit.
- ACT monitoring is used for heparinised stent deployment where appropriate.
- For prolonged spinal-risk procedures add continuous or repeated neurological assessment, and CSF drainage/MEP/SSEP according to the planned protection protocol.

## 4.4 Deployment and endograft-specific hazards

- The patient must remain motionless during the critical release.
- Anticipate transient hypotension or rapid ventricular pacing if requested for a precise landing; clarify how long it will last and how to immediately restore perfusion.
- Distinguish the brief intentional reduction in arterial pulsatility for deployment from prolonged low perfusion of the spinal cord or kidneys.
- Other hazards include access rupture, retroperitoneal haemorrhage, aortic injury, stent malposition, embolisation, arrhythmia and sudden loss of leg flow.
- Following deployment confirm systemic pressure, distal pulses, renal/visceral flow and aortic seal, and observe for neurologic deficits immediately when feasible.

### Endoleaks: why the type determines the response

| **Type** | **Mechanism** | **Clinical meaning** |
|---|---|---|
| I | Inadequate proximal (Ia) or distal (Ib) seal | Direct systemic-pressure flow into sac; generally demands prompt correction |
| II | Retrograde filling from side branches (e.g. lumbar/inferior mesenteric arteries) | Often observed if sac stable; persistent leak with sac growth may require treatment |
| III | Component separation or fabric tear | Direct flow into sac; usually urgent repair |
| IV | Graft-fabric porosity | Typically early, now uncommon; distinguish from serious types |
| V (endotension) | Sac expansion without visible leak | Requires investigation for occult leak, device failure and risk of rupture |

A completion angiogram without an obvious endoleak is not a substitute for long-term surveillance. Sac enlargement or late haemorrhage may reflect missed device failure. **Delayed rupture after EVAR remains a core limitation of the technique**, underpinning the long-term EVAR-1 findings [16].

## 4.5 TEVAR versus open thoracic or thoraco-abdominal repair

- Open descending thoracic and thoraco-abdominal aortic repair involves thoracotomy or thoracoabdominal exposure, cross-clamping, and possibly partial left-heart bypass/distal perfusion, selective visceral/renal perfusion, intercostal reimplantation and CSF drainage.
- The associated severe physiological stresses include one-lung ventilation, blood loss, high afterload, extensive distal ischaemia and large reperfusion load.
- TEVAR substantially reduces the burden of thoracotomy and cross-clamping but adds endograft-specific anatomical constraints and concerns about extensive segmental vessel coverage, arch embolisation, branch occlusion and spinal cord injury.
- The 2026 ESVS descending thoracic guidelines provide the current framework for selecting open, endovascular, staged or hybrid approaches [3].

- For thoracic repair, an apparently normal initial neurological exam does **not** exclude delayed spinal cord injury.
- Monitor lower-limb power as soon as possible and repeatedly, and avoid hypotension and anaemia during the high-risk postoperative period.
- Left subclavian revascularisation, preservation of hypogastric flow and staged extensive coverage help preserve collateral supply.
- The protective strategy is detailed in Chapter 5.

## 4.6 Complications after endovascular aortic repair and how to respond

- A patient can collapse from retroperitoneal bleeding without obvious drain output.
- Sudden hypotension, Hb fall, abdominal/back pain, groin swelling or metabolic acidosis after a large-bore femoral sheath should trigger assessment for aortic/iliac perforation or access-site bleeding, resuscitation and immediate procedural control.
- New acute leg pain or loss of pulses may be iliac-graft kinking, thrombosis, dissection or embolisation; Doppler and urgent vascular imaging/intervention follow.
- Severe AKI may reflect renal artery coverage or thrombosis.
- New paraplegia after TEVAR is an emergency: raise spinal perfusion pressure, consider urgent rescue CSF drainage and assess graft, bleeding and neurological alternatives without delay.
- New focal cortical deficit prompts stroke pathway and haemodynamic/embolism assessment.

- A contrast reaction may be non-allergic physiological (nausea, heat, vasovagal bradycardia) or anaphylactic.
- Hypotension with bronchospasm, airway swelling or circulatory compromise requires **immediate adrenaline and resuscitation** rather than a delayed antihistamine-first approach.
- Continue standard perioperative anaphylaxis investigation, including timed tryptase and specialist follow-up.
- Contrast extravasation causes soft tissue injury; manage according to severity, check compartment/neurovascular status and refer urgently if severe.
- High radiation exposures can produce delayed skin injury and need disclosure, dose review, documentation and specialist follow-up.
- Equipment-related and access injuries deserve the same incident review as theatre complications.

items.title: 5. Spinal cord protection in open aortic repair and TEVAR
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 5.1 Anatomy explains delayed as well as immediate paraplegia

- The spinal cord receives longitudinal supply from the anterior spinal artery (approximately anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries, supplemented by segmental radiculomedullary vessels.
- The dominant anterior radiculomedullary artery, often called the artery of Adamkiewicz, is variable but commonly arises on the left between T8 and L1.
- However, no single artery carries the entire burden; a network of intercostal, lumbar, vertebral/subclavian, internal iliac and paraspinal collaterals maintains flow.
- This network can remodel after staged vessel occlusion.
- Extensive aortic coverage or high cross-clamping can suddenly eliminate several inflows, while hypotension, anaemia and venous/CSF pressure reduce the residual network's effectiveness.

- The clinically useful equation is **spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) ≈ MAP − max(CSF pressure, relevant venous pressure)**.
- Raising MAP may not improve SCPP when CSF pressure is also markedly elevated.
- Equally, aggressive CSF drainage can cause subdural or intracranial bleeding.
- This explains why spinal protection is a bundle of haemodynamic, anatomical, monitoring and drainage decisions rather than a mandate to insert a lumbar drain in everyone.

## 5.2 Identify risk before the stent or clamp

- Risk increases with long-segment thoracic coverage, extent I–III thoracoabdominal aneurysm, prior infrarenal AAA repair (loss of lumbar collaterals), planned left subclavian coverage without revascularisation, poor internal iliac circulation, prolonged hypotension, anaemia, CKD, emergency repair, extensive segmental vessel sacrifice and long cross-clamp or operative times.
- Previous spinal cord injury and advanced atherosclerosis add vulnerability.
- Document baseline neurological function and existing motor deficits, and discuss expected spinal risk with the vascular team and patient.

### Core protocolised protective measures

- **Preserve collateral circulation:** consider left subclavian revascularisation when coverage is required, preserve internal iliac flow when feasible, consider intercostal reimplantation during open TAAA, minimise unnecessary aortic coverage and use staged repair for extensive endovascular reconstructions.
- **Protect oxygen delivery:** prevent prolonged hypotension and major anaemia.
  - For high-risk thoraco-abdominal repair, an example protocol is MAP about 90–100 mmHg (or higher when rescue is required), haemoglobin ≥100 g/L, adequate oxygenation and temperature control.
  - These are strategy-based targets rather than arbitrary thresholds for every small infrarenal EVAR.
- **Reduce surrounding pressure when appropriate:** lumbar CSF drainage in selected patients according to centre protocol, typically maintaining CSF pressure around ≤10–12 mmHg; drainage rate and daily maximum must be controlled to avoid intracranial haemorrhage.
- **Monitor:** early wake-up and frequent lower-limb motor examinations; MEPs and SSEPs in appropriate open/complex procedures, with anaesthesia tailored to maintain useful signals.
- **Rescue immediately:** an acute deficit is not something to “review on morning rounds.” Raise MAP, correct Hb/O₂, optimise cardiac output, urgently assess CSF pressure/drain feasibility and exclude graft occlusion, spinal haematoma or other structural causes.

## 5.3 The 2026 evidence changes who routinely receives a drain

- The 2026 ESVS guideline **strongly recommends prophylactic CSF drainage for open thoracic or thoraco-abdominal repair** (Class I, level A) but states that **selective reactive (rescue) drainage may be preferable to routine prophylactic drainage for extensive endovascular repair** (Class IIb, level C).
- This distinction reflects the RCT benefit in open TAAA repair and the real complication rate of lumbar drains in endovascular populations [3].
- It is incorrect to interpret “CSF drains prevent paraplegia” as proof that every TEVAR patient benefits from a prophylactic catheter.
- For selected very-high-risk endovascular anatomy, local protocols may still favour prophylaxis after multidisciplinary review.

- Why the difference?
- In the classic open TAAA trial, prophylactic drainage reduced permanent neurological injury, while modern endovascular strategies preserve or allow adaptation of collaterals by staging and often permit close neurological examination.
- Drain complications include bloody insertion, spinal/epidural haematoma, subdural/intracranial haemorrhage, overdrainage headache, infection, CSF leak and catheter failure.
- Anticoagulation is common in aortic repair, so insertion and removal require explicit antithrombotic timing and neurological surveillance.
- **A bloody or traumatic lumbar drain is a safety event:** reconsider systemic heparin timing, consult relevant teams and do not assume the catheter can safely function as planned.

## 5.4 Practical rescue algorithm for postoperative paraplegia

**Recognition:**

- Assess both lower limbs immediately after emergence and serially for at least the early high-risk period (often 48–72 h or longer for extensive repairs).
- A change in leg power, saddle sensation or sphincter function demands immediate action.
- Inspect hypotension episodes, Hb, oxygenation, temperature, K⁺/glucose, anticoagulation and drainage status.
- Rule out residual neuromuscular blockade and positioning injury, but do not delay perfusion rescue while deciding among diagnoses.

**Action:**

- Communicate with vascular, anaesthesia and ICU teams; restore MAP promptly (commonly ≥90 mmHg, often higher with deficit according to protocol), optimise CO and oxygenation, correct severe anaemia (many protocols target Hb ≥100 g/L), and ensure venous drainage is not obstructed.
- If a CSF catheter is already present, check pressure, blockage and controlled drainage against the prescribed target; if absent, urgently assess suitability for rescue insertion, taking anticoagulation and coagulopathy into account.
- Arrange spinal imaging as indicated to exclude compressive haematoma or structural pathology, and confirm graft and collateral vessel patency.
- Avoid excessively deep sedation that prevents serial motor examination.
- Repeated reassessment is essential: a rapidly improving deficit after raising SCPP suggests a potentially reversible perfusion problem, but does not eliminate later deterioration.

### Worked examination stem

- A patient develops bilateral leg weakness six hours after TEVAR covering 22 cm of aorta; Hb is 78 g/L, MAP 63 mmHg and no prophylactic drain was used.
- This should be approached as probable spinal cord hypoperfusion until proven otherwise, not attributed to residual anaesthetic.
- Simultaneously support MAP, correct oxygen delivery/anaemia, call the aortic team, assess the need and safety of rescue CSF drainage, and investigate alternative structural or vascular causes.
- **Do not give a large crystalloid bolus without considering myocardial function:** inadequate CO, bleeding and vasoplegia require different treatments.

items.title: 6. Acute aortic syndromes and aortic dissection: diagnosis, anti-impulse therapy and repair
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (3 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.los: SS_VS 1.10; SS_VS 1.12; IT_RT 1.2; SS_VS 1.7; SS_VS 1.19; SS_IC 1.34; SS_CS 1.6
items.body:
## 6.1 A dissection is not a ruptured aneurysm

- The immediate threat in **aortic dissection** is propagation of an intimal tear and false lumen under pulsatile stress.
- Complications depend on what that false lumen compresses or ruptures into: haemopericardium/tamponade, acute aortic regurgitation, coronary malperfusion, stroke, renal or mesenteric ischaemia, limb ischaemia and free rupture.
- The affected aortic segment changes the treatment.
- **Stanford type A** involves the ascending aorta, even if the entry tear is elsewhere; it is a cardiothoracic emergency.
- **Type B** does not involve the ascending aorta and is usually initially treated with anti-impulse therapy unless there is rupture, malperfusion, progression or other complication.
- A patient with uncomplicated acute type B dissection and BP 190/110 mmHg should not receive a major emergency operation simply because the diagnosis sounds dramatic.
- This is the exact error highlighted in the 2022.2 ANZCA examiner report [14].

- Distinguish classical dissection from **intramural haematoma** (bleeding into media without an obvious intimal flap) and **penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer** (ulceration through intima into media).
- These can progress to rupture or dissection.
- The same early impulse-control principles apply while anatomy and urgency are defined.
- Aortic aneurysm can coexist with any of these syndromes, but its presence does not convert the medical management of an uncomplicated type B dissection into permissive hypotension.

## 6.2 Clinical diagnosis: maintain suspicion while excluding competing catastrophes

- Classically there is abrupt severe chest or interscapular pain, sometimes tearing or migrating; abdominal pain, limb pain, syncope, stroke or acute paraplegia may dominate.
- Aortic regurgitation can present as a new diastolic murmur and shock; pericardial tamponade as sudden collapse.
- Differences in limb BP, pulse deficits, focal neurological signs and signs of visceral malperfusion support the diagnosis, but absence does not exclude it.
- Risk factors include chronic hypertension, connective tissue aortopathy (e.g. Marfan/Loeys–Dietz), bicuspid aortic valve/aneurysm, prior instrumentation, aortic surgery, stimulant use and pregnancy in susceptible patients.

- **CTA from chest through abdomen/pelvis**, according to local protocol, is the usual definitive test in a stable patient: identify ascending involvement, entry/re-entry, true/false lumen, branch-vessel perfusion, aneurysm and rupture.
- TEE is valuable when unstable or in theatre and can identify proximal flap, tamponade, acute AR and coronary involvement, but distal extent may be incompletely seen.
- TTE may detect tamponade or ascending dilatation but a negative examination does not exclude dissection.
- ECG and troponin may suggest ACS because dissection itself can cause coronary malperfusion; uncritical thrombolysis or anticoagulation for presumed ACS could be catastrophic.
- Chest radiography is neither sensitive nor specific.
- Blood counts, creatinine, lactate, blood group and coagulation guide complications and treatment, not exclusion of the diagnosis.

## 6.3 Initial anti-impulse therapy: control the slope of pressure rise as well as the pressure

- Aortic wall stress is driven not only by peak pressure but by the speed and force of LV ejection (**dP/dt**).
- Vasodilating a patient before rate control may provoke reflex tachycardia and increase shear stress even if the monitor shows a lower BP.
- Therefore, give titrated IV β-blockade first unless contraindicated, analgesia early, and add an arterial vasodilator only if the target pressure remains high.
- Provide invasive pressure monitoring and an appropriate high-dependency/ICU environment.
- The 2022 ACC/AHA aortic guideline recommends an **SBP below 120 mmHg, or the lowest pressure preserving organ perfusion, and HR 60–80/min** in acute aortic syndromes [4].
- In many stable patients a lower HR near 60 is desirable, but a fixed HR or SBP must not worsen shock or critical malperfusion.

### Drugs and physiology

- **IV esmolol:** readily titratable, short acting; for example 500 micrograms/kg loading over a minute if tolerated followed by 50 micrograms/kg/min, adjusted in steps (sometimes to 200–300 micrograms/kg/min) to HR and perfusion. A bolus is often omitted in a frail or marginally perfused patient.
- **IV labetalol:** combined β- and α-blockade with longer effect; e.g. initial 5–20 mg IV bolus repeated judiciously or a protocolised infusion; avoid overshoot bradycardia and low-output shock.
- **If β-blockers contraindicated:** non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker (e.g. IV diltiazem) for rate control in selected patients, avoiding use in severe LV systolic failure or conduction disease.
- **Once rate controlled:** add nicardipine, clevidipine or carefully titrated sodium nitroprusside for persistent hypertension, balancing cyanide/thiocyanate accumulation risk if prolonged nitroprusside is used in renal/hepatic failure.
  - Do **not** give a potent direct vasodilator in isolation when tachycardia remains uncontrolled.
- **Analgesia and nausea relief:** IV opioid titrated to pain and haemodynamics reduces sympathetic drive; avoid agitation, repeated coughing, severe hypercapnia and large procedural stress.

- For a 75-year-old with type B dissection and BP 190/110, establish arterial pressure and monitoring, treat severe pain, titrate esmolol toward HR near 60–80 and subsequently lower SBP toward <120 if organ perfusion tolerates it; assess creatinine, urine output, pulses, lactate and neurological findings.
- Aggressive lowering to SBP 90 in a patient with critical renal/visceral malperfusion may worsen injury, so targets are individualised with the aortic team.
- If the patient is already hypotensive, rapidly evaluate rupture, tamponade, severe AR or malperfusion; **do not follow a hypertension algorithm when the presentation has changed to shock**.

## 6.4 Indications and timing for intervention

**Type A:**

- Urgent operative repair after focused stabilisation.
- Typical surgical steps are median sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass via a safe arterial inflow site, cooling/cerebral protection as required, replacement of the ascending aorta ± hemiarch/arch and repair/replacement of the aortic valve/root when involved.
- The team may use antegrade cerebral perfusion and hypothermic circulatory arrest depending on arch anatomy.
- The anaesthetist anticipates major bleeding, malperfusion, dynamic AR, tamponade, coagulopathy, cerebral injury and prolonged postoperative organ support.
- Cannulation strategy and aortic pathology must be known before induction.
- Haemodynamically unstable type A disease needs urgent surgery rather than prolonged optimisation.

**Type B uncomplicated:**

- Initial medical management with imaging, analgesia and impulse control; repeat assessment for progression or high-risk anatomy and determine a follow-up plan.
- **Complicated type B:** rupture, refractory pain or hypertension despite treatment, rapid expansion, end-organ malperfusion or threatened organ/limb viability generally prompts urgent intervention, commonly TEVAR where anatomically suitable.
- Selected uncomplicated but high-risk type B patients may undergo delayed/subacute TEVAR following multidisciplinary assessment; the goal is not to rush every type B dissection to stent before the acute inflammatory phase has evolved.
- The 2026 ESVS descending aorta guideline distinguishes uncomplicated, high-risk and complicated disease and supports anatomy- and risk-dependent timing [3].

### True-lumen and branch-vessel obstruction

- Static obstruction occurs when the dissection flap extends into a branch and fixes a stenosis/occlusion; dynamic obstruction occurs when high false-lumen pressure compresses the true lumen or covers a branch opening.
- TEVAR sealing of the proximal entry tear may depressurise the false lumen and expand true-lumen flow, relieving dynamic malperfusion.
- Persistent static obstruction can still require branch stenting/fenestration or additional intervention.
- This explains why a successful-looking thoracic stent does not eliminate the need to recheck renal, bowel and leg perfusion.

## 6.5 Anaesthesia for TEVAR in type B dissection

- Before anaesthesia, confirm anticipated left subclavian coverage, access anatomy, rupture/malperfusion status, need for lumbar drain, heparin policy and the intended landing zone.
- Preserve haemodynamic stability during induction and ensure arterial access and ready vasopressor/vasodilator infusions.
- Avoid uncontrolled hypertension (risk of propagation) and prolonged hypotension (spinal, renal or cerebral malperfusion).
- The deployment phase may require transient reduction in pulsatility; restore MAP promptly after deployment.
- Assess pulses, urine output and metabolic status.
- Carefully consider **systemic heparin in a patient with active bleeding, traumatic brain injury or expanding haematoma**; this is an individualised vascular–anaesthetic decision, not an automatic 100 units/kg instruction.

- Complications specifically worth anticipating include access rupture, retrograde type A dissection, endograft-induced new entry tear, stroke, spinal cord injury, left arm ischaemia or posterior-circulation stroke after subclavian coverage, renal/visceral malperfusion, contrast-associated AKI and persistent false-lumen pressurisation.
- The initial postoperative plan should include serial neurovascular observations, sustained appropriate BP, renal/lactate assessment and follow-up imaging.

## 6.6 Open type A dissection repair: surgical sequence and anaesthetic responsibilities

- **This section closes the explicit SS_CS 1.5 surgical-steps and SS_CS 1.6 anaesthetic-principles components.** A ruptured aneurysm, stable uncomplicated type B dissection, and unstable ascending type A dissection have different induction and circulatory goals.
- In type A, tamponade, coronary malperfusion, acute severe aortic regurgitation (AR) or end-organ hypoperfusion may make standard antihypertensive/β-blocker titration dangerous.
- Summon cardiothoracic surgery, perfusion, blood bank and critical care early; time to definitive repair is the priority.

### Typical operative sequence (extent is anatomy-dependent)

- **1.** Review CTA/TEE for the proximal tear, true lumen, arch branch vessels, root/valve involvement, coronary ostia and pericardial blood; choose an arterial inflow site that avoids cannulating the false lumen or worsening malperfusion. Axillary, innominate, direct aortic or femoral strategies are selected by anatomy and expertise, not automatically by a single rule [4].

- **2.** Establish arterial/venous cannulation and cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), using systemic heparinisation and confirming adequate oxygen delivery and perfusion. Sternotomy and decompression of tamponade are dangerous before control is available; in extremis, the team may require selected cannulation or support before opening.

- **3.** Cool and protect the brain/viscera as required; cross-clamp and arrest the heart to inspect the tear and proximal aorta. Replace the ascending segment with a vascular graft; perform valve resuspension, root reconstruction or valve/root replacement if dictated by severe AR, root destruction or coronary involvement.

- **4.** For an open distal anastomosis and/or arch extension, use a team-selected period of circulatory arrest with appropriate temperature and antegrade/other cerebral perfusion where indicated. Hemiarch is often sufficient when the arch has no relevant tear or aneurysm; total arch/frozen elephant trunk is reserved for appropriate anatomy or malperfusion [4].

- **5.** Re-establish distal flow, de-air the graft and heart, rewarm and wean from CPB; assess repair, aortic valve, LV/RV function and regional perfusion by TEE, then reverse heparin with protamine, manage coagulopathy and achieve surgical haemostasis before transfer to ICU.

### Anaesthetic priorities by phase

**Before induction:**

- Plan two reliable arterial pressure sites when limb/arch branch malperfusion may make one misleading; large-bore access, crossmatched blood, rapid transfusion, vasoactives, TEE, cerebral oximetry where used, defibrillation and full CPB readiness.
- In severe tamponade or low-output shock, preserve spontaneous circulation and sympathetic compensation during carefully titrated induction while surgeons are immediately ready for rescue.
- Severe acute AR favours avoiding marked bradycardia and high afterload, whereas uncontrolled hypertension in a stable patient requires impulse control.
- These competing lesions demand a physiology-led rather than protocol-only induction.

**During CPB/repair:**

- Confirm adequate arterial inflow and systemic/cerebral perfusion (including arch branch considerations), communicate the planned temperature/flow/cerebral-protection strategy, monitor acid–base, lactate, potassium, Hb, glucose and temperature, and anticipate massive blood loss and complex coagulopathy.
- TEE can clarify AR, ventricular function, tamponade and postoperative repair but does not alone guarantee distal organ or cerebral protection.
- **Weaning and ICU:** assess residual AR, regional wall-motion abnormalities/coronary malperfusion, stroke, bleeding and tamponade, malperfusion of kidneys/bowel/limbs, vasoplegia, rhythm disturbance and postoperative mechanical circulatory support needs.
- Plan sedation, ventilation, anticoagulant restart and an explicit organ-perfusion surveillance schedule.

items.title: 7. Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: an integrated emergency operation
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 7.1 The natural history is rapid haemorrhage, not a routine elective pathway

- Rupture often presents with abdominal/back/flank pain, hypotension, collapse or a pulsatile mass, but the classic triad is frequently incomplete.
- Contained retroperitoneal rupture may allow brief relative stability; loss of tamponade can cause sudden exsanguination.
- Maintain a broad differential including other sources of haemorrhage, ACS, renal colic and intra-abdominal catastrophe.
- Bedside ultrasound may identify an aneurysm but **cannot reliably prove or exclude rupture**; CTA usually guides repair in a patient who can tolerate the transfer and rapid study, whereas the patient in extremis may go directly to the prepared hybrid theatre or operating room by local protocol.

- Early survival depends on prompt definitive proximal control, realistic resuscitation and a well-coordinated vascular–anaesthetic–radiology–blood-bank team.
- Avoid numerous transfers, investigations or invasive procedures that delay haemorrhage control.
- Reversal of anticoagulation and activation of MHP may be life-saving; obtain two large-bore IVs or appropriate rapid access, arterial pressure monitoring only if it does not delay control, temperature control, crossmatched blood and a clear plan for rescue aortic occlusion.

## 7.2 Controlled resuscitation: permissive hypotension before haemostasis

- Before proximal control, aggressive crystalloid-induced “normalisation” of BP can disrupt tamponade, increase bleeding, dilute coagulation factors and worsen acidosis/hypothermia.
- The 2024 ESVS guideline recommends permissive hypotension in conscious, adequately perfused patients with rupture, suggesting an SBP of approximately **70–90 mmHg**, with evidence graded level C [2].
- This is not a target for a deteriorating unconscious patient, a patient with catastrophic coronary hypoperfusion or after aortic control; it is an approach that tolerates lower pressure while prioritising rapid definitive repair and haemostatic blood resuscitation.
- Consciousness and ability to speak can indicate tolerable cerebral perfusion but are imperfect.
- Avoid deliberately lowering BP with nitrates outside a specific specialist protocol.

- Give blood and components early when needed.
- A major haemorrhage pack supplies RBCs, plasma and platelets with ratio-led early therapy until results permit targeted replacement; follow local practice.
- Reassess fibrinogen, ionised calcium, temperature, pH, K⁺, Hb and viscoelastic results.
- Avoid large crystalloid volumes except for an immediately demonstrated volume need when blood is unavailable.
- Reconcile the conflict: **before control avoid over-resuscitation; after control aim for adequate organ perfusion and oxygen delivery**.

## 7.3 Why the induction or conversion to GA is a dangerous moment

- With active retroperitoneal tamponade, the patient's sympathetic tone supports perfusion.
- Loss of this tone at induction can cause profound hypotension, and intubation/positive-pressure ventilation reduce venous return.
- Invasive monitoring and ideal airway optimisation are valuable only to the extent that they do not delay sealing the rupture.
- Have surgeons scrubbed and vascular access/control ready before induction when possible.
- Discuss whether a proximal occlusion balloon may be required and who will deploy it.

- If anatomy and cooperation permit, **emergency EVAR under local infiltration with minimal sedation** may preserve haemodynamics and is favoured by contemporary ESVS guidance when tolerated.
- Deep sedation may paradoxically recreate the problems of GA without a secured airway.
